name: Agag king of the Amalekites
charge: The sword that made women childless; and the sworn war with Amalek from generation to generation
summary: Amalek, Esau’s grandson, was the first nation to come against Israel after Egypt, and he did not meet the mighty men in front: he struck the rearmost, the feeble, when Israel was faint and weary, and he did not fear God. The Lord swore that He would have war with Amalek from generation to generation, and hundreds of years later He sent Saul to finish it. Saul spared the king, presuming to find something good in what God had condemned. Agag came to Samuel delicately, saying surely the bitterness of death was past, and the old prophet hewed him in pieces before the Lord at Gilgal.
offenseFull: Then came Amalek and fought with Israel in Rephidim (Exodus 17:8). Amalek was the first nation to come against Israel after Egypt, and he was Esau’s grandson, born to Eliphaz by Timna the concubine, and a duke in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:12). Moses gave the detail of the attack, and it was written to stir Israel up: remember what Amalek did by the way, how he met them and smote the hindmost, all that were feeble behind, when they were faint and weary, and he feared not God; and when the Lord gave them rest from all their enemies round about they were to blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven and not forget it (Deuteronomy 25:17-19). In a caravan the strong men walk in front; at the back are the elderly, the women, the babies and the lame. Amalek did not come at the front; he came up behind and waited until Israel was worn out. The Lord told Moses to write it in a book for a memorial and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, and He swore that He would have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Exodus 17:14-16). God does not forget; we do. Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High said remember, and the law against bearing a grudge is toward the children of our own people, not toward the nations He has sworn against (Leviticus 19:18).

Hundreds of years later the Lord sent Saul by Samuel, saying that He remembered what Amalek did to Israel when they came up from Egypt, and commanding him to go and smite Amalek and utterly destroy all that they had and spare them not (1 Samuel 15:1-3). The generation under that sword had not personally done the deed in the wilderness, which answers the argument heard today, that I never did anything to you; the Most High Himself commanded recompense for what was done to the forefathers. He also discriminates righteously: the Kenites were told to get down from among the Amalekites, because they had shown kindness to all the children of Israel when they came up out of Egypt. But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen and of the fatlings and the lambs, and destroyed only what was vile and refuse (1 Samuel 15:6-9). Agag was an Edomite king out of the line of the dukes of Esau, and Saul presumed to find something good in what God had condemned; he kept the one they liked, as men today keep the one Edomite at
work who smiles at them. Agag’s own charge is written into his sentence: his sword had made women childless.
judgmentFull: Samuel called for Agag the king of the Amalekites to be brought to him, and Agag came to him delicately, saying surely the bitterness of death was past (1 Samuel 15:32). With Saul under rebuke he figured nobody was angry at the Amalekites any more and he was safe. Never trust an enemy; though he humble himself and go crouching, his wickedness is as rusting brass, so take good heed and beware of him (Ecclesiasticus 12:10-11). Saul trusted the enemy; Samuel did not. The prophet told him that as his sword had made women childless, so his mother would be childless among women, and he hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal, measure for measure, finishing the commandment himself (1 Samuel 15:33). Samuel followed instructions; Saul played games. Because the line was not finished, in Esther’s day Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite rose out of that same seed and sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus (Esther 3:1); the war truly runs from generation to generation, and Esau keeps the records while we forget. Slaughter is prepared for the children of the wicked for the iniquity of their fathers, that the name and the remnant be cut off (Isaiah 14:21), and the same seed now says it is Jews and is not, but is the synagogue of Satan (Revelation 2:9). Understand the frame: as much as lies in us, we live peaceably with all men (Romans 12:18), we lay hands on no one, and we neither incite nor condone violence. The day when the man who rewards Babylon as she served us is called happy has not come (Psalms 137:8); it belongs to the return of the Lord, and it is His judgment written in His book, not a licence for any man’s hand now. The war continues, and it is more spiritual than ever.

text.text: Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim.
And Timna was concubine to Eliphaz Esau’s son; and she bare to Eliphaz Amalek: these were the sons of Adah Esau’s wife.
Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt;
How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.

Therefore it shall be, when the Lord thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.
And the Lord said unto Moses, Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.
And Moses built an altar, and called the name of it JEHOVAH–nissi:
For he said, Because the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.
Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord.
Samuel also said unto Saul, The Lord sent me to anoint thee to be king over his people, over Israel: now therefore hearken thou unto the voice of the words of the Lord.
Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt.
Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.

And Saul said unto the Kenites, Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel, when they came up out of Egypt. So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites.
And Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah until thou comest to Shur, that is over against Egypt.
And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword.

But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them: but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.
Then said Samuel, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites. And Agag came unto him delicately. And Agag said, Surely the bitterness of death is past.
Never trust thine enemy: for like as iron rusteth, so is his wickedness.

Though he humble himself, and go crouching, yet take good heed and beware of him, and thou shalt be unto him as if thou hadst wiped a lookingglass, and thou shalt know that his rust hath not been altogether wiped away.
And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal.
After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him.
Prepare slaughter for his children for the iniquity of their fathers; that they do not rise, nor possess the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities.
I know thy works, and tribulation, and poverty, (but thou art rich) and I know the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed; happy shall he be, that rewardeth thee as thou hast served us.
Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt.
Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.
